communicates.speaker: dr_mortimer
communicates.content: The recent sudden death of Sir Charles Baskerville, whose name has been mentioned as the probable Liberal candidate for Mid-Devon at the next election, has cast a gloom over the county. Though Sir Charles had resided at Baskerville Hall for a comparatively short period his amiability of character and extreme generosity had won the affection and respect of all who had been brought into contact with him. In these days of nouveaux riches it is refreshing to find a case where the scion of an old county family which has fallen upon evil days is able to make his own fortune and to bring it back with him to restore the fallen grandeur of his line. Sir Charles made large sums of money in South African speculation. He realised his gains and returned to England with them. It is only two years since he took up his residence at Baskerville Hall, and large schemes of reconstruction and improvement were interrupted by his death. Being childless, it was his desire that the whole countryside should profit by his good fortune. His generous donations to local and county charities have been frequently chronicled. The circumstances connected with the death of Sir Charles cannot be said to have been entirely cleared up by the inquest, but enough has been done to dispose of rumours. There is no reason whatever to suspect foul play, or to imagine that death could be from any but natural causes. Sir Charles was a widower and in some ways of an eccentric habit of mind. His indoor servants at Baskerville Hall consisted of a married couple named Barrymore, the husband acting as butler and the wife as housekeeper. Their evidence, corroborated by that of several friends, tends to show that Sir Charles's health has for some time been impaired, and points especially to some affection of the heart, manifesting itself in changes of colour, breathlessness, and acute attacks of nervous depression. Dr. James Mortimer, the friend and medical attendant of the deceased, has given evidence to the same effect.

Dr. Mortimer recounts the discovery and examination of Sir Charles Baskerville's body

communicates.speaker: dr_mortimer
communicates.content: On the night of Sir Charles’s death Barrymore the butler, who made the discovery, sent Perkins the groom on horseback to me, and as I was sitting up late I was able to reach Baskerville Hall within an hour of the event. I checked and corroborated all the facts which were mentioned at the inquest. I followed the footsteps down the yew alley, I saw the spot at the moor-gate where he seemed to have waited, I remarked the change in the shape of the prints after that point, I noted that there were no other footsteps save those of Barrymore on the soft gravel, and finally I carefully examined the body, which had not been touched until my arrival. Sir Charles lay on his face, his arms out, his fingers dug into the ground, and his features convulsed with some strong emotion to such an extent that I could hardly have sworn to his identity. There was certainly no physical injury of any kind. But one false statement was made by Barrymore at the inquest. He said that there were no traces upon the ground round the body. He did not observe any. But I did—some little distance off, but fresh and clear. Footprints. They were the footprints of a gigantic hound.

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: You saw this? And you said nothing? How was it that no one else saw it? There are many sheep-dogs on the moor? You say it was large? But it had not approached the body? What sort of night was it? But not actually raining? What is the alley like? Is there anything between the hedges and the walk? I understand that the yew hedge is penetrated at one point by a gate? Is there any other opening? So that to reach the yew alley one either has to come down it from the house or else to enter it by the moor-gate? Had Sir Charles reached this? Now, tell me, Dr. Mortimer—and this is important—the marks which you saw were on the path and not on the grass? Were they on the same side of the path as the moor-gate? Was the wicket-gate closed? How high was it? Then anyone could have got over it? And what marks did you see by the wicket-gate? Did no one examine? And found nothing? How do you know that? But the marks?

communicates.speaker: dr_mortimer
communicates.content: As clearly as I see you. What was the use? The marks were some twenty yards from the body and no one gave them a thought. I don’t suppose I should have done so had I not known this legend. No doubt, but this was no sheep-dog. Enormous. No. Damp and raw. No. There are two lines of old yew hedge, twelve feet high and impenetrable. The walk in the centre is about eight feet across. Yes, there is a strip of grass about six feet broad on either side. Yes, the wicket-gate which leads on to the moor. None. There is an exit through a summer-house at the far end. No; he lay about fifty yards from it. No marks could show on the grass. Yes; they were on the edge of the path on the same side as the moor-gate. Closed and padlocked. About four feet high. Yes. None in particular. Yes, I examined, myself. It was all very confused. Sir Charles had evidently stood there for five or ten minutes. Because the ash had twice dropped from his cigar. He had left his own marks all over that small patch of gravel. I could discern no others.

events.label: Holmes reacts with excitement and laments not being called in
Dr. Mortimer explains why he did not call Holmes in

communicates.speaker: dr_mortimer
communicates.content: I could not call you in, Mr. Holmes, without disclosing these facts to the world, and I have already given my reasons for not wishing to do so. Besides, besides— There is a realm in which the most acute and most experienced of detectives is helpless. You mean that the thing is supernatural?

events.label: Dr. Mortimer explains that several people had seen a creature on the moor before the tragedy

communicates.speaker: dr_mortimer
communicates.content: Since the tragedy, several incidents have come to my ears; before the terrible event occurred, several people had seen a creature upon the moor that corresponds with the Baskerville demon, could not possibly be any animal known to science, was huge, luminous, ghastly, and spectral, and there is a reign of terror in the district.

events.label: Holmes says he has confined his investigations to this world

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: I have hitherto confined my investigations to this world. In a modest way I have combated evil, but to take on the Father of Evil himself would, perhaps, be too ambitious a task. Yet you must admit that the footmark is material.

events.label: Mortimer says the original hound was material and diabolical

communicates.speaker: dr_mortimer
communicates.content: The original hound was material enough to tug a man’s throat out, and yet he was diabolical as well.

events.label: Holmes questions why Mortimer has come to consult him

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: I see that you have quite gone over to the supernaturalists. But now, Dr. Mortimer, tell me this. If you hold these views, why have you come to consult me at all? You tell me in the same breath that it is useless to investigate Sir Charles’s death, and that you desire me to do it. Then, how can I assist you?

events.label: Mortimer says Sir Henry Baskerville is arriving at Waterloo Station and asks what to do with him

communicates.speaker: dr_mortimer
communicates.content: By advising me as to what I should do with Sir Henry Baskerville, who arrives at Waterloo Station in exactly one hour and a quarter.

events.label: Mortimer identifies Sir Henry Baskerville as the heir and describes the family succession

communicates.speaker: dr_mortimer
communicates.content: Yes. On the death of Sir Charles we inquired for this young gentleman and found that he had been farming in Canada. From the accounts which have reached us he is an excellent fellow in every way. I speak now not as a medical man but as a trustee and executor of Sir Charles’s will. None. The only other kinsman whom we have been able to trace was Rodger Baskerville, the youngest of three brothers of whom poor Sir Charles was the elder. The second brother, who died young, is the father of this lad Henry. The third, Rodger, was the black sheep of the family. He made England too hot to hold him, fled to Central America, and died there in 1876 of yellow fever. Henry is the last of the Baskervilles. In one hour and five minutes I meet him at Waterloo Station. I have had a wire that he arrived at Southampton this morning. Now, Mr. Holmes, what would you advise me to do with him?

events.label: Holmes suggests that Sir Henry should go to the home of his fathers

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: Why should he not go to the home of his fathers?

events.label: Mortimer says every Baskerville who goes to the home meets with an evil fate and asks Holmes for advice

communicates.speaker: dr_mortimer
communicates.content: It seems natural, does it not? And yet, consider that every Baskerville who goes there meets with an evil fate. I feel sure that if Sir Charles could have spoken with me before his death he would have warned me against bringing this, the last of the old race, and the heir to great wealth, to that deadly place. And yet it cannot be denied that the prosperity of the whole poor, bleak countryside depends upon his presence. All the good work which has been done by Sir Charles will crash to the ground if there is no tenant of the Hall. I fear lest I should be swayed too much by my own obvious interest in the matter, and that is why I bring the case before you and ask for your advice.

events.label: Holmes recommends that Mortimer take a cab and meet Sir Henry Baskerville at Waterloo

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: I recommend, sir, that you take a cab, call off your spaniel who is scratching at my front door, and proceed to Waterloo to meet Sir Henry Baskerville.

events.label: Holmes instructs Mortimer to say nothing to Sir Henry until Holmes decides the matter

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: And then you will say nothing to him at all until I have made up my mind about the matter.

events.label: Mortimer agrees to Holmes's request to meet the next day with Sir Henry

communicates.speaker: dr_mortimer
communicates.content: I will do so, Mr. Holmes.

events.label: Mortimer leaves after scribbling the appointment on his shirt-cuff
Holmes stops Mortimer at the head of the stair and asks about the apparition on the moor

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: Only one more question, Dr. Mortimer. You say that before Sir Charles Baskerville’s death several people saw this apparition upon the moor?

events.label: Mortimer answers that three people saw the apparition before Sir Charles Baskerville's death and that he has not heard of any after

communicates.speaker: dr_mortimer
communicates.content: Three people did. I have not heard of any.

events.label: Holmes returns to his seat and resumes work on the case
Holmes asks Watson to go out, request tobacco from Bradley's, and not return before evening

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: Going out, Watson? Unless I can help you. No, my dear fellow, it is at the hour of action that I turn to you for aid. But this is splendid, really unique from some points of view. When you pass Bradley’s, would you ask him to send up a pound of the strongest shag tobacco? Thank you. It would be as well if you could make it convenient not to return before evening. Then I should be very glad to compare impressions as to this most interesting problem which has been submitted to us this morning.

events.label: Watson spends the day at his club and does not return to Baker Street until evening
Watson enters the sitting-room and finds it filled with tobacco smoke while Holmes smokes in an armchair
Sherlock Holmes comments on Watson's cold and the thick atmosphere

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: Caught cold, Watson? ... Open the window, then! You have been at your club all day, I perceive. Am I right?

events.label: Holmes laughs at Watson's bewildered expression
Holmes explains how he inferred Watson's movements and speaks about his own absence

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: There is a delightful freshness about you, Watson, which makes it a pleasure to exercise any small powers which I possess at your expense. A gentleman goes forth on a showery and miry day. He returns immaculate in the evening with the gloss still on his hat and his boots. He has been a fixture therefore all day. He is not a man with intimate friends. Where, then, could he have been? Is it not obvious? The world is full of obvious things which nobody by any chance ever observes. Where do you think that I have been? A fixture also. On the contrary, I have been to Devonshire. In spirit? Exactly. My body has remained in this armchair and has, I regret to observe, consumed in my absence two large pots of coffee and an incredible amount of tobacco. After you left I sent down to Stamford's for the Ordnance map of this portion of the moor, and my spirit has hovered over it all day. I flatter myself that I could find my way about. Very large.

events.label: Holmes unrolls a map section and indicates the district under discussion
Holmes discusses the possibility of supernatural forces and frames the questions of the case

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: It must be a wild place. The setting is a worthy one. If the devil did desire to have a hand in the affairs of men— The devil's agents may be of flesh and blood, may they not? There are two questions waiting for us at the outset. The one is whether any crime has been committed at all; the second is, what is the crime and how was it committed? Of course, if Dr. Mortimer's surmise should be correct, and we are dealing with forces outside the ordinary laws of Nature, there is an end of our investigation. But we are bound to exhaust all other hypotheses before falling back upon this one. I think we'll shut that window again, if you don't mind. It is a singular thing, but I find that a concentrated atmosphere helps a concentration of thought. I have not pushed it to the length of getting into a box to think, but that is the logical outcome of my convictions. Have you turned the case over in your mind?

events.label: Holmes discusses the footprints and the man's movement

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: It is very bewildering. It has certainly a character of its own. There are points of distinction about it. That change in the footprints, for example. Mortimer said that the man had walked on tiptoe down that portion of the alley. He only repeated what some fool had said at the inquest. Why should a man walk on tiptoe down the alley? What then? He was running, Watson—running desperately, running for his life, running until he burst his heart—and fell dead upon his face. Running from what? There lies our problem. There are indications that the man was crazed with fear before ever he began to run. I am presuming that the cause of his fears came to him across the moor. If that were so, and it seems most probable, only a man who had lost his wits would have run from the house instead of towards it. If the gipsy’s evidence may be taken as true, he ran with cries for help in the direction where help was least likely to be. Then, again, whom was he waiting for that night, and why was he waiting for him in the yew alley rather than in his own house? The man was elderly and infirm. We can understand his taking an evening stroll, but the ground was damp and the night inclement. Is it natural that he should stand for five or ten minutes, as Dr. Mortimer, with more practical sense than I should have given him credit for, deduced from the cigar ash? But he went out every evening. I think it unlikely that he waited at the moor-gate every evening. On the contrary, the evidence is that he avoided the moor. That night he waited there. It was the night before he made his departure for London. The thing takes shape, Watson. It becomes coherent. Might I ask you to hand me my violin, and we will postpone all further thought upon this business until we have had the advantage of meeting Dr. Mortimer and Sir Henry Baskerville in the morning.

events.label: Holmes asks Watson to hand him his violin

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: Might I ask you to hand me my violin

events.label: Holmes waits in his dressing-gown for the promised interview
Dr. Mortimer and Sir Henry Baskerville arrive for the appointment
Dr. Mortimer identifies the visitor as Sir Henry Baskerville

communicates.speaker: dr_mortimer
communicates.content: This is Sir Henry Baskerville.

events.label: Sir Henry says he would have come to Holmes on his own account

communicates.speaker: sir_henry_baskerville
communicates.content: The strange thing is, if my friend here had not proposed coming round to you this morning I should have come on my own account. I understand that you think out little puzzles, and I’ve had one this morning which wants more thinking out than I am able to give it.

events.label: Holmes invites Sir Henry to take a seat and asks about a remarkable experience in London

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: Pray take a seat, Sir Henry. Do I understand you to say that you have yourself had some remarkable experience since you arrived in London?

events.label: Sir Henry says the letter was the only matter of importance that morning

communicates.speaker: sir_henry_baskerville
communicates.content: Nothing of much importance, Mr. Holmes. Only a joke, as like as not. It was this letter, if you can call it a letter, which reached me this morning.

events.label: Sir Henry places the envelope on the table and the group examines it
Holmes asks who knew Sir Henry was going to the Northumberland Hotel

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: Who knew that you were going to the Northumberland Hotel?

events.label: Sir Henry says no one could have known and that they decided after he met Dr. Mortimer

communicates.speaker: sir_henry_baskerville
communicates.content: No one could have known. We only decided after I met Dr. Mortimer.

events.label: Dr. Mortimer says he had been staying with a friend

communicates.speaker: dr_mortimer
communicates.content: No, I had been staying with a friend.

events.label: Sir Henry says there was no possible indication that they intended to go to the hotel

communicates.speaker: sir_henry_baskerville
communicates.content: There was no possible indication that we intended to go to this hotel.

events.label: Holmes remarks that someone is deeply interested in Sir Henry's movements

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: Someone seems to be very deeply interested in your movements.

events.label: Holmes opens the folded paper from the envelope and spreads it on the table
Sir Henry asks Holmes for the meaning of the note

communicates.speaker: sir_henry_baskerville
communicates.content: Perhaps you will tell me, Mr. Holmes, what in thunder is the meaning of that, and who it is that takes so much interest in my affairs?

events.label: Holmes asks Dr. Mortimer what he makes of the note

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: What do you make of it, Dr. Mortimer? You must allow that there is nothing supernatural about this, at any rate?

events.label: Dr. Mortimer replies that the note might come from someone convinced the business is supernatural

communicates.speaker: dr_mortimer
communicates.content: No, sir, but it might very well come from someone who was convinced that the business is supernatural.

events.label: Sir Henry sharply asks what business Holmes and Mortimer mean

communicates.speaker: sir_henry_baskerville
communicates.content: What business?

events.label: Holmes promises to share their knowledge before Sir Henry leaves the room

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: You shall share our knowledge before you leave this room, Sir Henry. I promise you that.

events.label: Holmes says he will confine discussion to the document and asks Watson for yesterday's Times

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: We will confine ourselves for the present with your permission to this very interesting document, which must have been put together and posted yesterday evening. Have you yesterday’s Times, Watson? Might I trouble you for it—the inside page, please, with the leading articles? Capital article this on free trade. Permit me to give you an extract from it.

events.label: Holmes asks Watson for his reaction

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: What do you think of that, Watson?

events.label: Holmes laughs and rubs his hands together
Holmes asks whether the sentiment is admirable

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: Don't you think that is an admirable sentiment?

events.label: Dr. Mortimer looks at Holmes with professional interest and Sir Henry looks at Watson puzzled
Sir Henry says they have strayed from the trail

communicates.speaker: sir_henry_baskerville
communicates.content: I don't know much about the tariff and things of that kind, but it seems to me we've got a bit off the trail so far as that note is concerned.

events.label: Holmes says they are on the trail and that Watson has not grasped the sentence's significance

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: On the contrary, I think we are particularly hot upon the trail, Sir Henry. Watson here knows more about my methods than you do, but I fear that even he has not quite grasped the significance of this sentence.

events.label: Watson says he sees no connection

communicates.speaker: watson
communicates.content: No, I confess that I see no connection.

events.label: Holmes explains that the sentence fragments were extracted from the quotation

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: And yet, my dear Watson, there is so very close a connection that the one is extracted out of the other. 'You,' 'your,' 'your,' 'life,' 'reason,' 'value,' 'keep away,' 'from the.' Don't you see now whence these words have been taken?

events.label: Sir Henry reacts to Holmes's deduction

communicates.speaker: sir_henry_baskerville
communicates.content: By thunder, you're right! Well, if that isn't smart!

events.label: Holmes says the cutting was done in one piece

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: If any possible doubt remained it is settled by the fact that 'keep away' and 'from the' are cut out in one piece.

events.label: Dr. Mortimer praises Holmes's deduction

communicates.speaker: dr_mortimer
communicates.content: Really, Mr. Holmes, this exceeds anything which I could have imagined. I could understand anyone saying that the words were from a newspaper; but that you should name which, and add that it came from the leading article, is really one of the most remarkable things which I have ever known. How did you do it?

events.label: Holmes compares identifying typefaces to identifying skulls

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: I presume, Doctor, that you could tell the skull of a negro from that of an Esquimau? Because that is my special hobby. The differences are obvious. The supra-orbital crest, the facial angle, the maxillary curve, the— But this is my special hobby, and the differences are equally obvious. There is as much difference to my eyes between the leaded bourgeois type of a Times article and the slovenly print of an evening half-penny paper as there could be between your negro and your Esquimau. The detection of types is one of the most elementary branches of knowledge to the special expert in crime, though I confess that once when I was very young I confused the Leeds Mercury with the Western Morning News. But a Times leader is entirely distinctive, and these words could have been taken from nothing else. As it was done yesterday the strong probability was that we should find the words in yesterday’s issue.

events.label: Sir Henry summarizes the cutting of the message

communicates.speaker: sir_henry_baskerville
communicates.content: Someone cut out this message with a scissors—

events.label: Holmes explains the letter's clues and composition

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: There are indications, but the clues have been carefully removed; the address is printed in rough characters; the Times is usually found only in highly educated hands; the letter was composed by an educated man posing as uneducated; the writing may be known or become known by you; the pasted words are uneven; 'Life' is out of place; the cutter may have been careless or agitated and in a hurry; the address may have been written in a hotel; the pen and ink suggest hotel writing; the message may be traced by searching hotel waste-paper baskets around Charing Cross for the remains of the mutilated Times leader.

events.label: Dr. Mortimer comments on Holmes's reasoning

communicates.speaker: dr_mortimer
communicates.content: We are coming now rather into the region of guesswork.

events.label: Holmes inspects the foolscap and finds nothing on it

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: Nothing. It is a blank half-sheet of paper, without even a water-mark upon it. I think we have drawn as much as we can from this curious letter; and now, Sir Henry, has anything else of interest happened to you since you have been in London?

events.label: Holmes asks whether anyone has followed or watched Sir Henry

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: You have not observed anyone follow or watch you? You have nothing else to report to us before we go into this matter? I think anything out of the ordinary routine of life well worth reporting.

events.label: Sir Henry replies about the inquiry

communicates.speaker: sir_henry_baskerville
communicates.content: Why, no, Mr. Holmes. I think not. I seem to have walked right into the thick of a dime novel. Why in thunder should anyone follow or watch me? Well, it depends upon what you think worth reporting.

events.label: Sir Henry smiles
Sir Henry says he has spent nearly all his time in the States and Canada and hopes losing a boot is not ordinary life in Britain

communicates.speaker: sir_henry_baskerville
communicates.content: I don’t know much of British life yet, for I have spent nearly all my time in the States and in Canada. But I hope that to lose one of your boots is not part of the ordinary routine of life over here.

events.label: Holmes asks whether Sir Henry has lost one of his boots

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: You have lost one of your boots?

events.label: Dr. Mortimer says the boot is only mislaid and will be found when Sir Henry returns to the hotel

communicates.speaker: dr_mortimer
communicates.content: My dear sir, it is only mislaid. You will find it when you return to the hotel. What is the use of troubling Mr. Holmes with trifles of this kind?

events.label: Holmes says he asked for anything outside the ordinary routine

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: Well, he asked me for anything outside the ordinary routine. Exactly, however foolish the incident may seem. You have lost one of your boots, you say?

events.label: Sir Henry explains that he put both boots outside his door, found only one in the morning, could not get sense from the boot-cleaner, and bought the pair in the Strand last night without wearing them

communicates.speaker: sir_henry_baskerville
communicates.content: Well, mislaid it, anyhow. I put them both outside my door last night, and there was only one in the morning. I could get no sense out of the chap who cleans them. The worst of it is that I only bought the pair last night in the Strand, and I have never had them on.

events.label: Holmes asks why Sir Henry put unworn boots out to be cleaned

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: If you have never worn them, why did you put them out to be cleaned?

events.label: Sir Henry says the boots were tan and unvarnished and that is why he put them out

communicates.speaker: sir_henry_baskerville
communicates.content: They were tan boots and had never been varnished. That was why I put them out.

events.label: Holmes asks whether on arriving in London yesterday Sir Henry went out and bought a pair of boots

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: Then I understand that on your arrival in London yesterday you went out at once and bought a pair of boots?

events.label: Sir Henry says he did shopping, went round with Dr. Mortimer, bought brown boots, paid six dollars, and had one stolen before wearing them

communicates.speaker: sir_henry_baskerville
communicates.content: I did a good deal of shopping. Dr. Mortimer here went round with me. You see, if I am to be squire down there I must dress the part, and it may be that I have got a little careless in my ways out West. Among other things I bought these brown boots—gave six dollars for them—and had one stolen before ever I had them on my feet.

events.label: Holmes remarks that stealing the boot seems useless and says he shares the belief that the missing boot will soon be found

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: It seems a singularly useless thing to steal. I confess that I share Dr. Mortimer’s belief that it will not be long before the missing boot is found.

events.label: Sir Henry says he has spoken enough and asks for a full account of what they are driving at

communicates.speaker: sir_henry_baskerville
communicates.content: And, now, gentlemen, it seems to me that I have spoken quite enough about the little that I know. It is time that you kept your promise and gave me a full account of what we are all driving at.

events.label: Holmes agrees the request is reasonable and asks Dr. Mortimer to tell his story

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: Your request is a very reasonable one. Dr. Mortimer, I think you could not do better than to tell your story as you told it to us.

events.label: Dr. Mortimer presents the whole case from his papers
Sir Henry listens to the narrative and exclaims in surprise
Sir Henry says he has come into an inheritance, has heard of the hound since childhood, did not take it seriously before, and cannot yet make clear his uncle's death

communicates.speaker: sir_henry_baskerville
communicates.content: Well, I seem to have come into an inheritance with a vengeance. Of course, I’ve heard of the hound ever since I was in the nursery. It’s the pet story of the family, though I never thought of taking it seriously before. But as to my uncle’s death—well, it all seems boiling up in my head, and I can’t get it clear yet. You don’t seem quite to have made up your mind whether it’s a case for a policeman or a clergyman.

events.label: Sir Henry says the hotel letter fits into the matter

communicates.speaker: sir_henry_baskerville
communicates.content: And now there’s this affair of the letter to me at the hotel. I suppose that fits into its place.

events.label: Dr. Mortimer says someone knows more about what goes on upon the moor than they do

communicates.speaker: dr_mortimer
communicates.content: It seems to show that someone knows more than we do about what goes on upon the moor.

events.label: Holmes says someone is not ill-disposed toward Sir Henry because they warn him of danger

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: that someone is not ill-disposed towards you, since they warn you of danger.

events.label: Sir Henry says the sender may have wanted to scare him away for their own purposes

communicates.speaker: sir_henry_baskerville
communicates.content: Or it may be that they wish, for their own purposes, to scare me away.

events.label: Holmes says that possibility is also possible and thanks Dr. Mortimer for introducing an interesting problem

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: Well, of course, that is possible also. I am very much indebted to you, Dr. Mortimer, for introducing me to a problem which presents several interesting alternatives.

events.label: Holmes says the practical question is whether Sir Henry should go to Baskerville Hall

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: But the practical point which we now have to decide, Sir Henry, is whether it is or is not advisable for you to go to Baskerville Hall.

events.label: Mortimer and Baskerville leave by the front door
Holmes changes into action and quickly gets ready to go out
Holmes and Watson go into the street
Holmes and Watson follow Mortimer and Baskerville along Oxford Street and Regent Street
Mortimer and Baskerville stop and look in a shop window
Holmes also stops and looks into the shop window
Holmes notices a hansom cab and starts after it
The cab driver is signaled and the cab speeds away down Regent Street
Holmes questions Watson about the man in the cab

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: Who was the man? A spy?

events.label: Holmes explains that Baskerville has been shadowed in town

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: It was evident from what we have heard that Baskerville has been very closely shadowed by someone since he has been in town. How else could it be known so quickly that it was the Northumberland Hotel which he had chosen? If they had followed him the first day I argued that they would follow him also the second. You may have observed that I twice strolled over to the window while Dr. Mortimer was reading his legend. I was looking out for loiterers in the street, but I saw none. We are dealing with a clever man, Watson. This matter cuts very deep, and though I have not finally made up my mind whether it is a benevolent or a malevolent agency which is in touch with us, I am conscious always of power and design.

events.label: Holmes follows Dr. Mortimer and his companion

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: When our friends left I at once followed them in the hopes of marking down their invisible attendant. So wily was he that he had not trusted himself upon foot, but he had availed himself of a cab so that he could loiter behind or dash past them and so escape their notice. His method had the additional advantage that if they were to take a cab he was all ready to follow them. It puts him in the power of the cabman.

events.label: Watson regrets not getting the cab number

communicates.speaker: watson
communicates.content: What a pity we did not get the number!

events.label: Holmes states that cab 2704 is the man

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: My dear Watson, clumsy as I have been, you surely do not seriously imagine that I neglected to get the number? No. 2704 is our man. But that is no use to us for the moment.

events.label: Holmes explains how he should have followed the cab

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: I fail to see how you could have done more. On observing the cab I should have instantly turned and walked in the other direction. I should then at my leisure have hired a second cab and followed the first at a respectful distance, or, better still, have driven to the Northumberland Hotel and waited there. When our unknown had followed Baskerville home we should have had the opportunity of playing his own game upon himself and seeing where he made for. As it is, by an indiscreet eagerness, which was taken advantage of with extraordinary quickness and energy by our opponent, we have betrayed ourselves and lost our man.

events.label: Holmes observes that Dr. Mortimer and his companion have vanished

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: We had been sauntering slowly down Regent Street during this conversation, and Dr. Mortimer, with his companion, had long vanished in front of us. There is no object in our following them. The shadow has departed and will not return. We must see what further cards we have in our hands and play them with decision. Could you swear to that man’s face within the cab? And so could I—from which I gather that in all probability it was a false one. A clever man upon so delicate an errand has no use for a beard save to conceal his features. Come in here, Watson!

events.label: Holmes enters the district messenger office and is greeted by the manager

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: Ah, Wilson, I see you have not forgotten the little case in which I had the good fortune to help you? My dear fellow, you exaggerate. I have some recollection, Wilson, that you had among your boys a lad named Cartwright, who showed some ability during the investigation. thank you! And I should be glad to have change of this five-pound note.

events.label: Wilson responds to Holmes and confirms Cartwright is still with them

communicates.speaker: wilson
communicates.content: No, sir, indeed I have not. You saved my good name, and perhaps my life. My dear fellow, you exaggerate. I have some recollection, Wilson, that you had among your boys a lad named Cartwright, who showed some ability during the investigation. Yes, sir, he is still with us.

events.label: Holmes requests change for a five-pound note

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: thank you! And I should be glad to have change of this five-pound note.

events.label: Cartwright arrives and stands before Holmes
Holmes asks for the Hotel Directory

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: Let me have the Hotel Directory.

events.label: Holmes instructs Cartwright to visit the hotels and search for the page of the Times

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: There are the names of twenty-three hotels here, all in the immediate neighbourhood of Charing Cross. You will visit each of these in turn. You will begin in each case by giving the outside porter one shilling. Here are twenty-three shillings. You will tell him that you want to see the waste-paper of yesterday. You will say that an important telegram has miscarried and that you are looking for it. But what you are really looking for is the centre page of the Times with some holes cut in it with scissors. Here is a copy of the Times. It is this page. You could easily recognize it, could you not? In each case the outside porter will send for the hall porter, to whom also you will give a shilling. Here are twenty-three shillings. You will then learn in possibly twenty cases out of the twenty-three that the waste of the day before has been burned or removed. In the three other cases you will be shown a heap of paper and you will look for this page of the Times among it. The odds are enormously against your finding it. There are ten shillings over in case of emergencies. Let me have a report by wire at Baker Street before evening.

events.label: Holmes and Watson plan to find the cabman by wire and later go to picture galleries and the hotel
Sherlock Holmes inspects the hotel register
Holmes questions the porter about Theophilus Johnson and Mrs. Oldmore

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: Surely that must be the same Johnson whom I used to know; a lawyer, is he not, grey-headed, and walks with a limp? Surely you are mistaken about his trade? Mrs. Oldmore, too; I seem to remember the name. Excuse my curiosity, but often in calling upon one friend one finds another. Thank you; I am afraid I cannot claim her acquaintance.

events.label: Holmes and Watson go upstairs together while Holmes speaks in a low voice

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: We have established a most important fact by these questions, Watson. We know now that the people who are so interested in our friend have not settled down in his own hotel. That means that while they are very anxious to watch him, they are equally anxious that he should not see them. Now, this is a most suggestive fact.

events.label: Sir Henry Baskerville confronts Holmes and Watson with an old dusty boot
Sir Henry Baskerville complains about the missing boot

communicates.speaker: sir_henry_baskerville
communicates.content: Seems to me they are playing me for a sucker in this hotel. They’ll find they’ve started in to monkey with the wrong man unless they are careful. By thunder, if that chap can’t find my missing boot there will be trouble. I can take a joke with the best, Mr. Holmes, but they’ve got a bit over the mark this time.

events.label: Holmes asks whether Sir Henry is still looking for the boot

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: Still looking for your boot?

events.label: Sir Henry explains that his boot has changed from new brown to old black

communicates.speaker: sir_henry_baskerville
communicates.content: So it was, sir. And now it’s an old black one.

events.label: Holmes reacts in surprise to the boot account

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: What! you don’t mean to say—?

events.label: An agitated German waiter appears
A man reports that he has made inquiry all over the hotel but can hear no word of the missing boot.

communicates.speaker: unknown
communicates.content: No, sir; I have made inquiry all over the hotel, but I can hear no word of it.

events.label: A man threatens to leave the hotel unless the boot is returned before sundown and he can speak to the manager.

communicates.speaker: unknown
communicates.content: Well, either that boot comes back before sundown or I’ll see the manager and tell him that I go right straight out of this hotel.

events.label: A man promises that the boot will be found if given patience.

communicates.speaker: unknown
communicates.content: It shall be found, sir—I promise you that if you will have a little patience it will be found.

events.label: A man says he will lose no more property in the hotel.

communicates.speaker: unknown
communicates.content: Mind it is, for it’s the last thing of mine that I’ll lose in this den of thieves.

events.label: A man excuses himself to Holmes for troubling him about a trifle.

communicates.speaker: unknown
communicates.content: Well, well, Mr. Holmes, you’ll excuse my troubling you about such a trifle—

events.label: Holmes says the matter is well worth troubling about.

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: I think it’s well worth troubling about.

events.label: A man says he does not attempt to explain the matter and calls it the maddest, queerest thing that ever happened to him.

communicates.speaker: unknown
communicates.content: I just don’t attempt to explain it. It seems the very maddest, queerest thing that ever happened to me.

events.label: Holmes remarks that the case is very complex and that several threads may guide them to the truth.

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: I don’t profess to understand it yet. This case of yours is very complex, Sir Henry. When taken in conjunction with your uncle’s death I am not sure that of all the five hundred cases of capital importance which I have handled there is one which cuts so deep. But we hold several threads in our hands, and the odds are that one or other of them guides us to the truth. We may waste time in following the wrong one, but sooner or later we must come upon the right.

events.label: Holmes asks Baskerville about his intentions.

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: What were your intentions?

events.label: Sir Henry says he will go to Baskerville Hall at the end of the week.

communicates.speaker: sir_henry_baskerville
communicates.content: To go to Baskerville Hall. At the end of the week.

events.label: Holmes says he thinks Sir Henry's decision is wise and that unknown people are dogging him in London.

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: On the whole, I think that your decision is a wise one. I have ample evidence that you are being dogged in London, and amid the millions of this great city it is difficult to discover who these people are or what their object can be. If their intentions are evil they might do you a mischief, and we should be powerless to prevent it.

events.label: Holmes asks Dr. Mortimer whether he knew he was followed that morning from Holmes's house.

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: You did not know, Dr. Mortimer, that you were followed this morning from my house?

events.label: Dr. Mortimer starts violently.
Dr. Mortimer asks who followed him.

communicates.speaker: dr_mortimer
communicates.content: Followed! By whom?

events.label: Holmes says he cannot tell who followed Dr. Mortimer.

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: That, unfortunately, is what I cannot tell you.

events.label: Holmes asks whether any neighbour or acquaintance on Dartmoor has a black full beard.

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: Have you among your neighbours or acquaintances on Dartmoor any man with a black, full beard?

events.label: Dr. Mortimer names Barrymore as a man with a full black beard and says he is in charge of the Hall.

communicates.speaker: dr_mortimer
communicates.content: No—or, let me see—why, yes. Barrymore, Sir Charles’s butler, is a man with a full, black beard. He is in charge of the Hall.

events.label: Holmes says they had best ascertain whether Barrymore is at the Hall or possibly in London.

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: Ha! Where is Barrymore? We had best ascertain if he is really there, or if by any possibility he might be in London.

events.label: Holmes asks for a telegraph form and composes telegrams to Barrymore and the Grimpen postmaster.

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: Is all ready for Sir Henry? Address to Mr. Barrymore, Baskerville Hall. Send a second wire to the postmaster, Grimpen: 'Telegram to Mr. Barrymore to be delivered into his own hand. If absent, please return wire to Sir Henry Baskerville, Northumberland Hotel.'

events.label: Dr. Mortimer says Barrymore is the son of the old caretaker, who is dead, and that the Barrymores have looked after the Hall for four generations.

communicates.speaker: dr_mortimer
communicates.content: He is the son of the old caretaker, who is dead. They have looked after the Hall for four generations now. So far as I know, he and his wife are as respectable a couple as any in the county.

events.label: Baskerville says the Barrymores have a fine home and nothing to do while no family member is at the Hall.

communicates.speaker: sir_henry_baskerville
communicates.content: At the same time, it’s clear enough that so long as there are none of the family at the Hall these people have a mighty fine home and nothing to do.

events.label: Holmes asks whether Barrymore profited from Sir Charles's will

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: Did Barrymore profit at all by Sir Charles’s will?

events.label: It is stated that Barrymore and his wife receive five hundred pounds each under Sir Charles's will

communicates.speaker: barrymore
communicates.content: He and his wife had five hundred pounds each.

events.label: Holmes asks whether Barrymore and his wife knew they would receive the money

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: Did they know that they would receive this?

events.label: It is stated that Sir Charles often talked about the provisions of his will

communicates.speaker: barrymore
communicates.content: Yes; Sir Charles was very fond of talking about the provisions of his will.

events.label: Dr. Mortimer states that he received a thousand pounds under Sir Charles's will

communicates.speaker: dr_mortimer
communicates.content: I also had a thousand pounds left to me.

events.label: Holmes asks whether anyone else received a legacy

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: And anyone else?

events.label: Dr. Mortimer states that many small sums and public charities were included in the will

communicates.speaker: dr_mortimer
communicates.content: There were many insignificant sums to individuals, and a large number of public charities. The residue all went to Sir Henry.

events.label: Holmes asks how much the residue was

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: And how much was the residue?

events.label: Dr. Mortimer states that the residue was seven hundred and forty thousand pounds

communicates.speaker: dr_mortimer
communicates.content: Seven hundred and forty thousand pounds.

events.label: Holmes reacts with surprise at the size of the sum

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: I had no idea that so gigantic a sum was involved.

events.label: Dr. Mortimer explains the estate's value and Sir Charles's wealth

communicates.speaker: dr_mortimer
communicates.content: Sir Charles had the reputation of being rich, but we did not know how very rich he was until we came to examine his securities. The total value of the estate was close on to a million.

events.label: Holmes comments that the sum is enough to tempt desperate action

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: It is a stake for which a man might well play a desperate game.

events.label: Holmes asks who would inherit the estate

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: who would inherit the estate?

events.label: Dr. Mortimer states that after Rodger Baskerville's death the estate would descend to the Desmonds

communicates.speaker: dr_mortimer
communicates.content: Since Rodger Baskerville, Sir Charles’s younger brother died unmarried, the estate would descend to the Desmonds, who are distant cousins. James Desmond is an elderly clergyman in Westmoreland.

events.label: Holmes asks whether Dr. Mortimer has met Mr. James Desmond

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: Have you met Mr. James Desmond?

events.label: Dr. Mortimer states that James Desmond once visited Sir Charles and refused a settlement

communicates.speaker: dr_mortimer
communicates.content: Yes; he once came down to visit Sir Charles. He is a man of venerable appearance and of saintly life. I remember that he refused to accept any settlement from Sir Charles, though he pressed it upon him.

events.label: Holmes remarks that the heir would be entitled to Sir Charles's wealth

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: And this man of simple tastes would be the heir to Sir Charles’s thousands.

events.label: Dr. Mortimer explains that James Desmond would inherit the entailed estate and possibly the money

communicates.speaker: dr_mortimer
communicates.content: He would be the heir to the estate because that is entailed. He would also be the heir to the money unless it were willed otherwise by the present owner, who can, of course, do what he likes with it.

events.label: Holmes asks whether Sir Henry has made his will

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: And have you made your will, Sir Henry?

events.label: Sir Henry states that he has not made his will

communicates.speaker: sir_henry_baskerville
communicates.content: No, Mr. Holmes, I have not. I’ve had no time, for it was only yesterday that I learned how matters stood. But in any case I feel that the money should go with the title and estate. That was my poor uncle’s idea. How is the owner going to restore the glories of the Baskervilles if he has not money enough to keep up the property? House, land, and dollars must go together.

events.label: Holmes advises Sir Henry to go to Devonshire without delay

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: I am of one mind with you as to the advisability of your going down to Devonshire without delay.

events.label: Holmes states that Sir Henry must not go alone and should take a trusty man

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: There is only one provision which I must make. You certainly must not go alone. Dr. Mortimer returns with me. But Dr. Mortimer has his practice to attend to, and his house is miles away from yours. With all the goodwill in the world he may be unable to help you. No, Sir Henry, you must take with you someone, a trusty man, who will be always by your side.

events.label: Sir Henry asks whether Holmes could come himself

communicates.speaker: sir_henry_baskerville
communicates.content: Is it possible that you could come yourself, Mr. Holmes?

events.label: Holmes states that he cannot go to Dartmoor for an indefinite time

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: If matters came to a crisis I should endeavour to be present in person; but you can understand that, with my extensive consulting practice and with the constant appeals which reach me from many quarters, it is impossible for me to be absent from London for an indefinite time. At the present instant one of the most revered names in England is being besmirched by a blackmailer, and only I can stop a disastrous scandal. You will see how impossible it is for me to go to Dartmoor.

events.label: Holmes recommends Watson as a companion for the trip

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: If my friend would undertake it there is no man who is better worth having at your side when you are in a tight place. No one can say so more confidently than I.

events.label: Baskerville grips Watson's hand and asks him to come to Baskerville Hall

communicates.speaker: sir_henry_baskerville
communicates.content: Well, now, that is real kind of you, Dr. Watson. You see how it is with me, and you know just as much about the matter as I do. If you will come down to Baskerville Hall and see me through I’ll never forget it.

events.label: Watson agrees to come to Baskerville Hall

communicates.speaker: watson
communicates.content: I will come, with pleasure. I do not know how I could employ my time better.

events.label: Holmes instructs Watson to report carefully and to be ready by Saturday

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: And you will report very carefully to me. When a crisis comes, as it will do, I will direct how you shall act. I suppose that by Saturday all might be ready?

events.label: The group agrees to meet at the ten-thirty train from Paddington on Saturday

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: Then on Saturday, unless you hear to the contrary, we shall meet at the ten-thirty train from Paddington.

events.label: Baskerville finds his missing brown boot under a cabinet
Holmes remarks that the boot has returned easily

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: May all our difficulties vanish as easily!

events.label: Mortimer comments on the boot's appearance and says he searched the room before lunch

communicates.speaker: dr_mortimer
communicates.content: But it is a very singular thing. I searched this room carefully before lunch.

events.label: Baskerville says he also searched the room and that the boot was not there then

communicates.speaker: sir_henry_baskerville
communicates.content: And so did I. Every inch of it. There was certainly no boot in it then.

events.label: Holmes suggests the waiter placed the boot there while they were lunching

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: In that case the waiter must have placed it there while we were lunching.

events.label: The German is sent for and questioned about the boot

communicates.speaker: the_german
communicates.content: I know nothing of the matter.

events.label: Holmes and Watson drive back to Baker Street in a cab
Holmes sits in thought through the afternoon and evening
Two telegrams are handed in before dinner
Holmes states that Barrymore is at the Hall and that Cartwright failed to trace the cut sheet of The Times

communicates.speaker: cartwright
communicates.content: Have just heard that Barrymore is at the Hall. Visited twenty-three hotels as directed, but sorry to report unable to trace cut sheet of The Times.

events.label: Holmes says he must seek another lead

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: There go two of my threads, Watson. There is nothing more stimulating than a case where everything goes against you. We must cast round for another scent.

events.label: Holmes says he has wired to learn the cabman's name and address

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: Exactly. I have wired to get his name and address from the Official Registry. I should not be surprised if this were an answer to my question.

events.label: The cabman's arrival at the door follows the bell ring
A cabman arrives and questions Holmes about what he has against him

communicates.speaker: the_cabman
communicates.content: I got a message from the head office that a gent at this address had been inquiring for No. 2704. I’ve driven my cab this seven years and never a word of complaint. I came here straight from the Yard to ask you to your face what you had against me.

events.label: Holmes offers the cabman money for answers and asks for his name and address

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: I have nothing in the world against you, my good man. On the contrary, I have half a sovereign for you if you will give me a clear answer to my questions. First of all your name and address, in case I want you again.

events.label: The cabman gives his name, address, and cab yard

communicates.speaker: the_cabman
communicates.content: John Clayton, 3 Turpey Street, the Borough. My cab is out of Shipley's Yard, near Waterloo Station.

events.label: Holmes makes a note of the cabman's details
Holmes asks the cabman about the fare who watched the house and followed the gentlemen

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: Tell me all about the fare who came and watched this house at ten o’clock this morning and afterwards followed the two gentlemen down Regent Street.

events.label: The cabman says the fare told him he was a detective and ordered silence

communicates.speaker: the_cabman
communicates.content: The gentleman told me that he was a detective and that I was to say nothing about him to anyone. Yes, he did. When he left me. He mentioned his name.

events.label: Holmes reacts with triumph and asks for the name mentioned

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: That was imprudent. What was the name that he mentioned?

events.label: The cabman identifies the fare as Mr. Sherlock Holmes

communicates.speaker: the_cabman
communicates.content: His name was Mr. Sherlock Holmes.

events.label: Holmes laughs and remarks on the cabman's touch

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: A touch, Watson—an undeniable touch! I feel a foil as quick and supple as my own. He got home upon me very prettily that time. So his name was Sherlock Holmes, was it?

events.label: The cabman confirms the name

communicates.speaker: the_cabman
communicates.content: Yes, sir, that was the gentleman’s name.

events.label: Holmes asks where the cabman picked up the fare and what occurred

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: Tell me where you picked him up and all that occurred.

events.label: The cabman describes picking up the fare in Trafalgar Square and following two gentlemen by cab

communicates.speaker: the_cabman
communicates.content: He hailed me at half-past nine in Trafalgar Square. He said that he was a detective, and he offered me two guineas if I would do exactly what he wanted all day and ask no questions. I was glad enough to agree. First we drove down to the Northumberland Hotel and waited there until two gentlemen came out and took a cab from the rank. We followed their cab until it pulled up somewhere near here. This very door. We pulled up halfway down the street and waited an hour and a half. Then the two gentlemen passed us, walking, and we followed down Baker Street and along— Until we got three-quarters down Regent Street. Then my gentleman threw up the trap, and he cried that I should drive right away to Waterloo Station as hard as I could go. I whipped up the mare and we were there under the ten minutes. Then he paid up his two guineas, like a good one, and away he went into the station. Only just as he was leaving he turned round and he said: ‘It might interest you to know that you have been driving Mr. Sherlock Holmes.’ That’s how I come to know the name.

events.label: The cabman answers that he saw no more of Holmes after Holmes went into the station

communicates.speaker: the_cabman
communicates.content: Not after he went into the station.

events.label: The cabman describes Holmes’s appearance

communicates.speaker: the_cabman
communicates.content: Well, he wasn’t altogether such an easy gentleman to describe. I’d put him at forty years of age, and he was of a middle height, two or three inches shorter than you, sir. He was dressed like a toff, and he had a black beard, cut square at the end, and a pale face. I don’t know as I could say more than that. No, I can’t say that. No, sir; nothing.

events.label: Holmes gives the cabman half-sovereigns and dismisses him

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: Well, then, here is your half-sovereign. There’s another one waiting for you if you can bring any more information. Good-night!

events.label: John Clayton departs chuckling
Holmes turns to Watson and comments on the investigation

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: Snap goes our third thread, and we end where we began. The cunning rascal! He knew our number, knew that Sir Henry Baskerville had consulted me, spotted who I was in Regent Street, conjectured that I had got the number of the cab and would lay my hands on the driver, and so sent back this audacious message. I tell you, Watson, this time we have got a foeman who is worthy of our steel. I’ve been checkmated in London. I can only wish you better luck in Devonshire. But I’m not easy in my mind about it. About sending you. It’s an ugly business, Watson, an ugly dangerous business, and the more I see of it the less I like it. Yes, my dear fellow, you may laugh, but I give you my word that I shall be very glad to have you back safe and sound in Baker Street once more.

events.label: Sir Henry Baskerville and Dr. Mortimer depart for Devonshire
Holmes drives Watson to the station and gives parting instructions

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: I will not bias your mind by suggesting theories or suspicions, Watson; I wish you simply to report facts in the fullest possible manner to me, and you can leave me to do the theorizing. Anything which may seem to have a bearing however indirect upon the case, and especially the relations between young Baskerville and his neighbours or any fresh particulars concerning the death of Sir Charles. I have made some inquiries myself in the last few days, but the results have been negative. One thing only appears to be certain, and that is that Mr. James Desmond, who is the next heir, is an elderly gentleman of a very amiable disposition, so that this persecution does not arise from him. I really think that we may eliminate him entirely from our calculations. There remain the people who will actually surround Sir Henry Baskerville upon the moor. By no means. You could not make a greater mistake. If they are innocent it would be a cruel injustice, and if they are guilty we should be giving up all chance of bringing it home to them. No, no, we will preserve them upon our list of suspects. Then there is a groom at the Hall, if I remember right. There are two moorland farmers. There is our friend Dr. Mortimer, whom I believe to be entirely honest, and there is his wife, of whom we know nothing. There is this naturalist, Stapleton, and there is his sister, who is said to be a young lady of attractions. There is Mr. Frankland, of Lafter Hall, who is also an unknown factor, and there are one or two other neighbours. These are the folk who must be your very special study. You have arms, I suppose? Most certainly. Keep your revolver near you night and day, and never relax your precautions.

events.label: Watson says he has taken his arms

communicates.speaker: watson
communicates.content: Yes, I thought it as well to take them.

events.label: Sir Henry and Dr. Mortimer wait on the platform with a first-class carriage
Dr. Mortimer reports that they have no news and have not been shadowed

communicates.speaker: dr_mortimer
communicates.content: We have no news of any kind. We have not been shadowed during the last two days. We have never gone out without keeping a sharp watch, and no one could have escaped our notice.

events.label: Holmes asks whether Sir Henry and Dr. Mortimer have always kept together

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: You have always kept together, I presume?

events.label: Dr. Mortimer explains that he spent yesterday afternoon at the Museum of the College of Surgeons

communicates.speaker: dr_mortimer
communicates.content: Except yesterday afternoon. I usually give up one day to pure amusement when I come to town, so I spent it at the Museum of the College of Surgeons.

events.label: Sir Henry says he went to look at the folk in the park

communicates.speaker: sir_henry_baskerville
communicates.content: I went to look at the folk in the park.

events.label: Holmes warns Sir Henry not to go about alone and to avoid the moor at night

communicates.speaker: sherlock_holmes
communicates.content: It was imprudent, all the same. I beg, Sir Henry, that you will not go about alone. Some great misfortune will befall you if you do. Did you get your other boot? Indeed. That is very interesting. Well, good-bye. Bear in mind, Sir Henry, one of the phrases in that queer old legend which Dr. Mortimer has read to us, and avoid the moor in those hours of darkness when the powers of evil are exalted.

events.label: Holmes stands motionless on the platform as the train leaves
The speaker plays with Dr. Mortimer’s spaniel during the journey
The landscape changes as the train travels through Devon
Sir Henry Baskerville stares out of the window and cries aloud with delight
Sir Henry Baskerville says he has never seen a place to compare with Devon

communicates.speaker: sir_henry_baskerville
communicates.content: I’ve been over a good part of the world since I left it, Dr. Watson, but I have never seen a place to compare with it.

events.label: Watson remarks that Devonshire men swear by their county

communicates.speaker: watson
communicates.content: I never saw a Devonshire man who did not swear by his county.

events.label: Dr. Mortimer replies that it depends on the breed of men as much as on the county

communicates.speaker: dr_mortimer
communicates.content: It depends upon the breed of men quite as much as on the county.

events.label: Dr. Mortimer comments on a friend’s Celtic head type and Sir Charles’s mixed Gaelic and Ivernian type

communicates.speaker: dr_mortimer
communicates.content: A glance at our friend here reveals the rounded head of the Celt, which carries inside it the Celtic enthusiasm and power of attachment. Poor Sir Charles’s head was of a very rare type, half Gaelic, half Ivernian in its characteristics.

events.label: Dr. Mortimer asks whether Sir Henry was very young when he last saw Baskerville Hall

communicates.speaker: dr_mortimer
communicates.content: But you were very young when you last saw Baskerville Hall, were you not?

events.label: Sir Henry says he was a boy when his father died, never saw the Hall, left for America, and is eager to see the moor

communicates.speaker: sir_henry_baskerville
communicates.content: I was a boy in my teens at the time of my father’s death and had never seen the Hall, for he lived in a little cottage on the South Coast. Thence I went straight to a friend in America. I tell you it is all as new to me as it is to Dr. Watson, and I’m as keen as possible to see the moor.

events.label: Dr. Mortimer points out the first sight of the moor

Any number of them are ready to swear that they have seen such a creature upon the moor. The story took a great hold upon the imagination of Sir Charles, and I have no doubt that it led to his tragic end. His nerves were so worked up that the appearance of any dog might have had a fatal effect upon his diseased heart. I fancy that he really did see something of the kind upon that last night in the yew alley. I feared that some disaster might occur, for I was very fond of the old man, and I knew that his heart was weak. My friend Mortimer told me. You think, then, that some dog pursued Sir Charles, and that he died of fright in consequence? Have you any better explanation? Has Mr. Sherlock Holmes? It is useless for us to pretend that we do not know you, Dr. Watson. The records of your detective have reached us here, and you could not celebrate him without being known yourself. When Mortimer told me your name he could not deny your identity. If you are here, then it follows that Mr. Sherlock Holmes is interesting himself in the matter, and I am naturally curious to know what view he may take. I am afraid that I cannot answer that question. May I ask if he is going to honour us with a visit himself? He cannot leave town at present. He has other cases which engage his attention. If I had any indication of the nature of your suspicions or how you propose to investigate the case, I might perhaps even now give you some aid or advice. communicates.speaker: sir_henry_baskerville
communicates.content: We have made up our minds to have the truth out of you, so it will save you trouble to tell it sooner rather than later. Come, now! No lies! What were you doing at that window?

communicates.speaker: sir_henry_baskerville
communicates.content: Move your light across the window, Watson! See, the other moves also! Now, you rascal, do you deny that it is a signal? Come, speak up! Who is your confederate out yonder, and what is this conspiracy that is going on?

communicates.speaker: sir_henry_baskerville
communicates.content: Then you leave my employment right away. And you go in disgrace. By thunder, you may well be ashamed of yourself. Your family has lived with mine for over a hundred years under this roof, and here I find you deep in some dark plot against me.

events.label: Mrs. Barrymore enters the doorway and speaks to Sir Henry

communicates.speaker: mrs_barrymore
communicates.content: No, no, sir; no, not against you! We have to go, Eliza. This is the end of it. You can pack our things. Oh, John, John, have I brought you to this? It is my doing, Sir Henry—all mine. He has done nothing except for my sake and because I asked him.

events.label: Mrs. Barrymore explains the night light signals and Selden's hiding place

communicates.speaker: the_barrymore_woman
communicates.content: My unhappy brother is starving on the moor. We cannot let him perish at our very gates. The light is a signal to him that food is ready for him, and his light out yonder is to show the spot to which to bring it. The escaped convict, sir—Selden, the criminal. I said that it was not my secret and that I could not tell it to you. But now you have heard it, and you will see that if there was a plot it was not against you.

events.label: Mrs. Barrymore identifies Selden as her younger brother

communicates.speaker: the_barrymore_woman
communicates.content: Yes, sir, my name was Selden, and he is my younger brother. We humoured him too much when he was a lad and gave him his own way in everything until he came to think that the world was made for his pleasure, and that he could do what he liked in it. Then as he grew older he met wicked companions, and the devil entered into him until he broke my mother’s heart and dragged our name in the dirt. From crime to crime he sank lower and lower until it is only the mercy of God which has snatched him from the scaffold; but to me, sir, he was always the little curly-headed boy that I had nursed and played with as an elder sister would.

events.label: Mrs. Barrymore explains why Selden broke prison and was sheltered

communicates.speaker: the_barrymore_woman
communicates.content: That was why he broke prison, sir. He knew that I was here and that we could not refuse to help him. When he dragged himself here one night, weary and starving, with the warders hard at his heels, what could we do? We took him in and fed him and cared for him. Then you returned, sir, and my brother thought he would be safer on the moor than anywhere else until the hue and cry was over, so he lay in hiding there. But every second night we made sure if he was still there by putting a light in the window, and if there was an answer my husband took out some bread and meat to him. Every day we hoped that he was gone, but as long as he was there we could not desert him. That is the whole truth, as I am an honest Christian woman and you will see that if there is blame in the matter it does not lie with my husband but with me, for whose sake he has done all that he has.

events.label: Barrymore confirms Mrs. Barrymore's account

communicates.speaker: barrymore
communicates.content: Yes, Sir Henry. Every word of it.

communicates.speaker: sir_henry_baskerville
communicates.content: Well, I cannot blame you for standing by your own wife. Forget what I have said. Go to your room, you two, and we shall talk further about this matter in the morning.

For God's sake, sir, I beg of you not to let the police know that he is still on the moor. They have given up the chase there, and he can lie quiet until the ship is ready for him. communicates.content: He would not do anything so mad, sir. We have provided him with all that he can want. To commit a crime would be to show where he was hiding.

communicates.content: That is true. Well, Barrymore—

communicates.content: Do you know how he died?

communicates.speaker: barrymore
communicates.content: I know why he was at the gate at that hour. It was to meet a woman. Yes, sir.

communicates.speaker: sir_henry_baskerville
communicates.content: And the woman’s name?

communicates.content: I can’t give you the name, sir, but I can give you the initials. Her initials were L. L.

events.label: Sir Henry asks how Barrymore knows this

communicates.speaker: sir_henry_baskerville
communicates.content: How do you know this, Barrymore?

communicates.speaker: barrymore
communicates.content: Your uncle had a letter that morning. But that morning, as it chanced, there was only this one letter, so I took the more notice of it. It was from Coombe Tracey, and it was addressed in a woman’s hand.

communicates.speaker: barrymore
communicates.content: Well, sir, I thought no more of the matter, and never would have done had it not been for my wife. The greater part of it was charred to pieces, but one little slip, the end of a page, hung together, and the writing could still be read. It seemed to us to be a postscript at the end of the letter and it said: ‘Please, please, as you are a gentleman, burn this letter, and be at the gate by ten o clock. Beneath it were signed the initials L. L.’

communicates.speaker: sir_henry_baskerville
communicates.content: Have you got that slip?

communicates.speaker: barrymore

communicates.content: Had Sir Charles received any other letters in the same writing?

But now you have been kind to us, and I feel as if it would be treating you unfairly not to tell you all that I know about the matter.

events.label: Sir Henry dismisses Barrymore

communicates.speaker: sir_henry_baskerville
communicates.content: Very good, Barrymore; you can go.

communicates.content: It's all these goings-on, sir. There's foul play somewhere, and there's black villainy brewing, to that I’ll swear! Very glad I should be, sir, to see Sir Henry on his way back to London again!

communicates.speaker: watson
